description:
Every Moon mission begins with one decision: where and when to land. We are a passionate team committed to space exploration and well-crafted technology. Our project, LunaLens, turns lunar terrain and Sun and Earth position data into a clear tool for mission planners. We bring together web development, Python, data analysis, 3D visualization, and interface design. With our team in place, we are focused on delivering a prototype that mission planners can trust.

See you on the moon🚀
summary:
LunaLens is a web tool that helps mission planners choose where and when to land on the Moon. Landing is a problem of light and line of sight: sunlight must reach the solar arrays, and Earth must be in view for direct communication. Both change sharply with small shifts in site or date.

We built LunaLens to answer these questions in seconds. For any curated site (Apollo landing sites, CLPS targets, and other missions) or custom coordinates, it shows the Sun and Earth relative to the true local horizon, using NASA LOLA topography and JPL Horizons ephemerides. A Site Ranking Engine scores each site from 0 to 100 with a green, yellow or red status. A Sky Visibility Radar and Mission Timeline report sunlight duration and Earth visibility windows. An Astronaut Eye View shows, in first-person 3D, where terrain blocks the Sun or Earth.

LunaLens addresses the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by making site and date comparison fast and intuitive. It reports geometric visibility, not guaranteed power or radio performance.
details:
What it does and how it works

LunaLens lets a user pick a landing site, either from a curated list (Apollo landing sites, NASA CLPS targets, other commercial and national missions) or by entering custom coordinates, and choose a date or mission window. For that site and time, it computes where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the true local horizon. Terrain from NASA LOLA elevation data is used to test whether ridges block either body, and Sun and Earth positions come from JPL Horizons ephemerides.

A Python backend precomputes hourly results for each site and serves them through FastAPI, so every part of the interface reads the same data. Four connected features turn this geometry into decisions:

  • Site and Date Comparison: sites are compared side by side, so alternatives can be evaluated quickly when a launch is delayed.
  • Site Ranking Engine: each site receives a weighted 0-100 suitability score, led by sunlight and Earth visibility, with a per-criterion breakdown and a green, yellow or red status against mission requirements. Slope and roughness are included as terrain-safety criteria.
  • Sky Visibility Radar and Mission Timeline: these show solar elevation, sunlight duration, Earth visibility windows, and time remaining before sunset or Earthset. A slider and animation move through a lunar day or the whole mission.
  • Astronaut Eye View: an interactive first-person 3D scene at the chosen site and time, with the Sun and Earth placed in the sky and blocked by terrain where appropriate.

(If completed: an AI assistant explains sites, dates and scores, answering only from LunaLens's own computed results.)

Benefits and intended impact

The required data already exists, but it is spread across specialist tools such as Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons, which are hard to combine and interpret. LunaLens brings it into one guided tool, so planners can see which site ranks best, why, and when conditions are favorable. The traffic-light status gives an instant answer, and the 3D view builds an intuition that tables and maps cannot, such as how a ridge blocks Earth at a given hour. We aim to make early-stage site and date comparison faster and more accessible for mission planners, educators, and students, while keeping results transparent and reproducible through open NASA data.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NASA LOLA digital elevation models (LRO mission); JPL Horizons ephemeris system
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy / SciPy
  • Frontend: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS
  • 3D: Three.js and React Three Fiber
  • Collaboration: GitHub (feature branches and reviewed pull requests) and Discord
  • Optional: an LLM API for the assistant

Creativity

LunaLens combines three things that are usually separate: real local-horizon geometry, side-by-side site and date comparison, and a first-person view of the same data. Most illumination studies are static and site-specific, and most portals are built for experts. Treating the Sun and Earth relative to the terrain horizon, rather than a flat horizon or the Sun's centre alone, makes the results more realistic and easier to understand.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy and limits: the Moon has no atmosphere, so the horizon is set by terrain and the edge of the lunar sphere. LunaLens reports geometric visibility only, not guaranteed power generation or radio link performance, and we state this clearly.
  • Validation: results are compared with published data for known landing sites, and edge cases are tested.
  • Usability: the design targets non-specialists, with clear status colors, adjustable weights for different mission priorities, and answers within seconds.
  • Process: a phased plan in which each feature works standalone before integration, with the assistant started only after the integrated prototype exists.

Before submitting, adjust this to match what you actually built. For example, if you used a simplified terrain model or fewer sites than planned, say so, and remove the assistant line if it isn't working. I can also trim this to a specific word limit if the form has one.
